prize_parts.citation: for the development of targeted protein degradation, in which designed bifunctional molecules recruit E3 ubiquitin ligases to remove proteins that inhibitors cannot reach

statement.case_for: I keep my round-1 configuration: a single-part prize for targeted protein degradation by designed bifunctional molecules, credited to Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli. The achievement is a new chemical design principle, induced proximity, in which a small molecule converts ligase recruitment into destruction of a chosen protein. Crews and Deshaies established the concept in 2001, Crews made it a sustained programme, and Ciulli's VHL ligands and ternary-complex structural work turned it into a rational design discipline that many independent groups now apply. For me the decisive question is whether a discovery changed what researchers and clinicians can actually do, and here it plainly has: targets once called undruggable are now addressed in the laboratory and in late-stage clinical trials. Round 1 did not weaken the scientific case; every objection raised against it was about timing or attribution, not about whether the principle is real.
statement.case_against: Maturity and attribution remain the honest weaknesses. As far as I am aware no degrader is yet an approved drug, so the prize may be early on clinical consequence, and I have no current regulatory evidence to offer the chair beyond that. The three-name limit leaves out the thalidomide-cereblon molecular-glue line (Handa, Ito, Gray), where the mechanism was actually worked out, plus Sakamoto and Kim, and the citation must be worded so that it honours induced-proximity design by bifunctional molecules without implying that the glue mechanism is being credited or dismissed. The ubiquitin-proteasome prize of 2004 also needs a careful distinction. Aqvist is right that the missing approval is the main reason the committee might wait, and I now weigh it more heavily than I did in round 1, though not enough to change my position.

responses.point: Aqvist agrees with the Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli trio but argues that I treated the missing regulatory approval as a minor point and that the citation must cover induced proximity without crediting the whole molecular-glue story.
responses.response: I accept both corrections. Approval is the main maturity risk, not a footnote, and I will say so plainly. I still read the game-changer test as met on the evidence of validated mechanism, structural understanding of ternary complexes, independent reproduction and a large late-stage pipeline, which is more evidence of consequence than the nitrogenase or perovskite cases offer. I have narrowed my citation to designed bifunctional molecules recruiting E3 ligases so that it does not stretch to the glue mechanism, which I would leave to a later, separate discussion of Handa, Ito and Gray.

responses.point: Chabes holds that base editing is a distinct chemical invention rather than a CRISPR extension, because it replaces cleavage with deamination and needed an evolved TadA for adenine, that neither base editors nor degraders yet have an approved product, and that his real reservation about B011 is attribution.
responses.response: The deaminase and directed-evolution argument persuades me, and I withdraw the word extension: base editing is chemically distinct from cutting. I also concede that approval status does not separate the two candidates. What still separates them for me is breadth of consequence. Induced proximity is a whole modality, with ligase recruiters, linker design rules and a pipeline across many target classes, while base editing arrives six years after the 2020 prize and with Kondo and Nishida's priority question open. On attribution I think the Crews, Deshaies, Ciulli cut is the cleaner of the two: it follows the concept, the first rational ligase ligands and the structural logic, whereas the base editing cut excludes an independent parallel inventor. I keep B007 as my first alternative.

responses.point: Brzezinski argues that the PROTAC concept and the cereblon glue mechanism are different discoveries by different people, that three seats cannot honour both without a vague citation, and that the missing approval weighs on maturity.
responses.response: I agree these are two discoveries, and that is why I have narrowed the citation to bifunctional degraders instead of trying to cover both. A precise citation about designed molecules recruiting E3 ligases is not vague, and it leaves the glue mechanism open for later recognition, in the way earlier prizes have left neighbouring contributions to a later year. I do not dispute that the maturity concern is real. On nitrogenase, I still find the carbide structure impressive, but you yourself say the N2 binding mode is open and the Dean and Ribbe attribution is unresolved, so I cannot rank it above degradation.

responses.point: The chair asks whether base editing can be framed as distinct from the 2020 CRISPR prize and hold at three names, and whether a two-part prize could be explained to a general audience.
responses.response: I think base editing can be framed as distinct, and I would not oppose it, but the Target-AID question for Kondo and Nishida makes the three-name version less secure than the chair suggests. On a two-part prize, I do not see a pairing that shares a theme or a three-laureate limit without cutting names on both sides, and Somfai's combination of C-N coupling and a Liu-only base editing part loses coherence. A single well-defined achievement is easier to defend, so I stay with one part.

uncertainties: Whether a first PROTAC or molecular-glue degrader approval has occurred or is imminent, which I cannot verify from the materials provided
Whether the committee will accept a citation limited to bifunctional degraders while leaving out Handa, Ito and Gray
Whether base editing, with a stronger first-place count, will draw a majority despite the Kondo and Nishida question
Whether the committee regards degradation as sufficiently distinct from the 2004 ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis prize
statement.conflict_note: No recusal-level conflict. None of the shortlisted candidates is a mentor or collaborator of mine. My only disclosed connection is a field overlap with Emma Sparr on peptide-lipid and protein self-assembly, which bears on B046 alone and does not touch my preferred configuration.
